title: L'agent junior en priorité  (Junior Agent Priority)

segments.t: In Gabriel's office, Andrea is anxious after visiting Guy Marchand's doctor. Trying to shift focus to agency business, she asks Gabriel about recruiting a junior agent, but encounters unexpected hesitation. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Je sors de chez le médecin de Guy.
La santé de Guy est une catastrophe.
Tu veux me parler d'autre chose?
Oui, au sujet de l'agent junior.
Est-ce que tu en veux un?
Prendre un junior ne me fait pas peur.
Ton avis compte beaucoup pour moi.
Ce n'est pas ma priorité en ce moment.
Tu veux un garçon ou une fille?
Les deux me vont très bien.
Tu crois que ça va te rendre faible?
Je ne suis pas comme ça, Andréa.
Maintenant, j'ai beaucoup de travail.
Let's examine Andrea and Gabriel's private office discussion step by step to explore professional boundaries and vulnerabilities.
Je sors de chez le médecin de Guy.
'I have just come from Guy's doctor.' Because French has no apostrophe-s, 'Guy's doctor' becomes 'the doctor of Guy', preceded by 'from the office of'.
La santé de Guy est une catastrophe.
'Guy's health is a disaster.' Notice 'the health of Guy' — that word meaning 'health' is the very same one you'll hear in French toasts when clinking glasses.
Tu veux me parler d'autre chose?
'Do you want to talk about something else?' French says 'speak of other thing', contracting 'of' before 'other' to cover English 'about something else'.
Oui, au sujet de l'agent junior.
'Yes, about the junior agent.' Literally 'at the subject of', that three-word opener is a handy phrase meaning 'regarding' in workplace conversations, placing 'junior' after 'agent'.
Est-ce que tu en veux un?
'Do you want one?' Where English simply says 'want one', French slips a tiny 'of them' right before 'want' — literally 'do you of-them want one?'
Prendre un junior ne me fait pas peur.
'Taking on a junior does not scare me.' French starts with plain 'to take' rather than an '-ing' word, and 'scare me' is built from 'make fear to me'.
Ton avis compte beaucoup pour moi.
'Your opinion means a lot to me.' Word for word, Andrea says 'your opinion counts a lot for me', choosing a cousin of English 'advice' that means 'opinion' in French.
Ce n'est pas ma priorité en ce moment.
'It is not my priority right now.' At the end, 'in this moment' is the natural French expression for 'right now' or 'at the moment'.
Tu veux un garçon ou une fille?
'Do you want a boy or a girl?' Andrea keeps statement order and simply raises her pitch, joining the two choices with 'or' — pronounced just like the French question word meaning 'where'.
Les deux me vont très bien.
'Both suit me very well.' Instead of a separate single word meaning 'both', French says 'the two', and 'go very well to me' is how you'd say something suits you fine.
Tu crois que ça va te rendre faible?
'Do you think that will make you look weak?' When 'make' precedes a quality like 'weak', French reaches for a cousin of English 'render' — literally 'render you weak' — rather than 'do'.
Je ne suis pas comme ça, Andréa.
'I am not like that, Andrea.' Right before her name, 'like that' is a super reusable two-word chunk you can swap in for 'that way' or 'like this' in everyday talk.
Maintenant, j'ai beaucoup de travail.

'Right now, I have a lot of work.' Notice how 'I' drops its vowel and fuses onto 'have' via an apostrophe, followed by 'a lot of work' to politely end the chat. Now let's listen to the whole dialogue again.
Je sors de chez le médecin de Guy.
La santé de Guy est une catastrophe.
Tu veux me parler d'autre chose?
Oui, au sujet de l'agent junior.
Est-ce que tu en veux un?
Prendre un junior ne me fait pas peur.
Ton avis compte beaucoup pour moi.
Ce n'est pas ma priorité en ce moment.
Tu veux un garçon ou une fille?
Les deux me vont très bien.
Tu crois que ça va te rendre faible?
Je ne suis pas comme ça, Andréa.
Maintenant, j'ai beaucoup de travail.

Andrea and Gabriel navigate professional challenges and personal vulnerabilities as the agency faces major changes. Let's review the workplace and emotional vocabulary from this scene. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
